text:
Example 9.11: The Jackknife-after-Bootstrap Plot

jack.after.boot(boot.out, useJ = TRUE, stinf = FALSE)



For each left-out observation: percentiles of \(\hat\theta^* - \hat\theta\) (vertical) against the jackknife influence value (horizontal). Points far to the left/right are influential.

title: The Jackknife and Resampling Applications 🔪
section: Two Ways to Bootstrap a Regression
text:
Two Ways to Bootstrap a Regression


Resampling cases (pairs)

Resample rows \((x_i, y_i)\) with replacement; refit.
Robust to heteroscedasticity and model misspecification.
Treats \(X\) as random.


Resampling errors (residuals)

Fit; resample residuals \(\hat e_j^*\); set \(y_i^* = \hat y_i + \hat e^*_i\); refit.
Treats \(X\) as fixed; assumes the model and iid errors.
Use modified residuals \(r_i = \hat e_i/\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}\) (centered).

title: The Jackknife and Resampling Applications 🔪
text:
Examples 9.5 - 9.6: Resampling Cases (Iron Data)

L <- lm(magnetic ~ chemical, data = iron)
m <- 2000; n <- NROW(iron); L1 <- numeric(m); set.seed(4750)
for (b in 1:m) {
  i <- sample(1:n, replace = TRUE)
  L1[b] <- coef(lm(magnetic ~ chemical, data = iron[i, ]))[2]
}

set.seed(4750); boot.cases <- boot(iron, beta_case, R = 2000)
c(slope = coef(L)[2], se_lm = summary(L)$coef[2, 2], se_loop = sd(L1), se_boot = sd(boot.cases$t))

slope.chemical          se_lm        se_loop        se_boot

title: The Jackknife and Resampling Applications 🔪
text:
Examples 9.7 - 9.9: Resampling (Modified) Errors

y <- log(mammals$brain); x <- log(mammals$body)
L <- lm(y ~ x); n <- length(y)
r <- residuals(L) / sqrt(1 - hatvalues(L)); r <- r - mean(r)     # modified, centered residuals
set.seed(4750); m <- 2000; estsE <- numeric(m)
for (b in 1:m) {
  ystar <- fitted(L) + sample(r, replace = TRUE)
  estsE[b] <- coef(lm(ystar ~ x))[2]
}
model_based <- function(dat, i) { ystar <- dat$fit + dat$r[i]; coef(lm(ystar ~ dat$x))[2] }
dat <- data.frame(x = x, fit = fitted(L), r = r)
set.seed(4750); boot.err <- boot(dat, model_based, R = 2000)
c(slope = coef(L)[2], se_lm = summary(L)$coef[2, 2], se_errors = sd(estsE), se_boot_fn = sd(boot.err$t))

title: The Jackknife and Resampling Applications 🔪
text:
Influence (Rizzo 9.3)

The empirical influence value of \(x_i\) measures how much \(\hat\theta\) changes when \(x_i\) is up-weighted; the jackknife approximation is \(l_{\text{jack},i} = (n-1)(\hat\theta - \hat\theta_{(i)})\).
\(\sum_i l_i^2/n^2\) approximates \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)\) (the nonparametric delta method).

Example 9.10 (patch ratio):

L.inf <- empinf(boot.out, type = "jack")
round(L.inf, 4)

[1] -0.0993  0.4004 -0.3489  0.4280 -0.1445  0.0892 -0.0451 -0.3438

c(se_delta = sqrt(sum(L.inf^2)) / n, se_boot = sd(boot.out$t))

se_delta  se_boot 
 0.01274  0.10098

title: The Jackknife and Resampling Applications 🔪
text:
Summary


Jackknife: \(n\) leave-one-out replicates; \(\widehat\mathrm{bias}= (n-1)(\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)}-\hat\theta)\), \(\widehat\mathrm{se}= \sqrt{\tfrac{n-1}{n}\sum(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar{\hat\theta}_{(\cdot)})^2}\).
Exact for the mean; removes \(O(1/n)\) bias; fails for non-smooth statistics (use delete-\(d\) or the bootstrap).
Jackknife-after-bootstrap: SE of bootstrap estimates and influence diagnostics with no extra resampling.
Regression: resample cases (robust) or errors (model-based, use modified residuals).

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
section: Functional Data: Repeated Measures of a Smooth Process
text:
Functional Data: Repeated Measures of a Smooth Process



Data are measurements of smooth processes over a continuum (usually time).
We do not want parametric assumptions about those processes.
Often multiple curves of the same process; we describe the variation between curves.
Frequently high resolution and low noise.


“Functional data is multivariate data with an ordering on the dimensions.” (Müller, 2006)
\[
y_{ij} = x_i(t_{ij}) + \epsilon_{ij},\qquad x_i(t)\ \text{smooth}.
\]
Functional data = the functions \(x_i(t)\).

Applications: medical monitoring (EEG, ECG, fMRI), biology (growth curves), environmental monitoring (weather, pollution), traffic.

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Canadian Weather Data
Average daily temperature and precipitation at 35 Canadian weather stations (classical and much used).

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(day, temp, type = "l", lty = 1, col = adjustcolor("#2E5BBA", .5), xlab = "day", ylab = "deg C", main = "Temperature")
lines(day, temp[, "Vancouver"], lwd = 3, col = "red")
matplot(day, precip, type = "l", lty = 1, col = adjustcolor("#2E5BBA", .5), xlab = "day", ylab = "mm", main = "Precipitation")
lines(day, precip[, "Vancouver"], lwd = 3, col = "red")

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
section: Weather in Vancouver and the Challenges
text:
Weather in Vancouver and the Challenges

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(day, temp[, "Vancouver"], pch = 20, col = "#2E5BBA", xlab = "Day", ylab = "Temperature (deg C)", main = "Vancouver")
plot(day, precip[, "Vancouver"], pch = 1, col = "#2E5BBA", xlab = "Day", ylab = "Precipitation (mm)", main = "Vancouver")


Challenges: estimating functions from noisy discrete observations; numerical representation of infinite-dimensional objects; representing variation in infinite dimensions; relationships between functional objects; \(n < p = \infty\) (we need smoothness); measures of variation in estimates.

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
From Discrete to Functional Data
Two problems, two methods:

Represent non-parametric continuous-time functions: basis expansions \[
x(t) = \sum_{k=1}^K c_k\phi_k(t) = \boldsymbol\Phi(t)\mathbf c,\quad \phi_k \text{ pre-defined}.
\]
Reduce noise in measurements: smoothing penalties \[
\hat{\mathbf c} = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf c}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i - x(t_i)\big)^2 + \lambda\int[Lx(t)]^2dt,
\] where \(Lx\) measures the “roughness” of \(x\) (e.g. \(Lx = x''\)) and \(\lambda\) trades fit for smoothness.

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Basis Expansions Are Just Regression
From multiple regression \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{1i} + \cdots + \epsilon_i\), or with curvature \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1t_i + \beta_2t_i^2 + \cdots\). For one record, \(y_i = x(t_i) + \epsilon_i\) with \(x(t) = \boldsymbol\Phi(t)\mathbf c\):
\[
\hat{\mathbf c} = (\boldsymbol\Phi^\text{T}\boldsymbol\Phi)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Phi^\text{T}\mathbf{y},\qquad \hat\mathbf{y}= \mathbf{S}\mathbf{y},\ \ \mathbf{S}= \boldsymbol\Phi(\boldsymbol\Phi^\text{T}\boldsymbol\Phi)^{-1}\boldsymbol\Phi^\text{T}.
\]

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
section: The Monomial Basis and Its Problems
text:
The Monomial Basis and Its Problems
\(\boldsymbol\Phi(t) = (1, t, t^2, t^3, \dots)\)

y <- temp[, "Vancouver"]; tt <- day / 365
Phi_mono <- outer(tt, 0:7, `^`)
kappa(Phi_mono); kappa(cbind(1, poly(tt, 7)))            # monomials are badly conditioned (Ch 13)

[1] 160809


[1] 18.97

fit_mono <- lm(y ~ poly(tt, 7))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(day, Phi_mono[, 2:6], type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, ylab = "basis", main = "Monomial basis")
plot(day, y, pch = 20, col = "red", main = "Vancouver: degree 7 polynomial"); lines(day, fitted(fit_mono), lwd = 3, col = "#003366")



Monomial fits have derivatives that behave badly (the second derivative explodes at the ends), and the basis is nearly collinear.

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
The Fourier Basis
\[
1,\ \sin(\omega t),\ \cos(\omega t),\ \sin(2\omega t),\ \cos(2\omega t),\ \dots,\qquad \omega = 2\pi/P.
\]

fourier_basis <- function(t, K, P = 365) {
  B <- matrix(1, length(t), 1)
  for (k in 1:K) B <- cbind(B, sin(2 * pi * k * t / P), cos(2 * pi * k * t / P))
  B
}
Phi_f <- fourier_basis(day, 3)
fit_f <- lm.fit(Phi_f, y)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(day, Phi_f[, 2:5], type = "l", lty = c(1, 2, 1, 2), col = c(2, 4, 2, 4), lwd = 2, ylab = "", main = "Fourier basis (k = 1, 2)")
plot(day, y, pch = 20, col = "red", main = "Vancouver: 7 Fourier functions"); lines(day, Phi_f %*% fit_f$coefficients, lwd = 3, col = "#003366")



Advantages: excellent computational properties (orthogonal on equally spaced points; FFT), natural for periodic data. But representations are periodic: a problem if the data are not.

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Spline Bases
Truncated power basis of degree \(d\) with knots \(\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_K\): \[
1, t, \dots, t^d, (t-\kappa_1)_+^d, \dots, (t-\kappa_K)_+^d.
\] Piecewise polynomials, joined smoothly (\(d-1\) continuous derivatives) at the knots. B-splines span the same space with a well-conditioned, compactly supported basis.

library(splines)
kn <- seq(0, 365, length = 9)[-c(1, 9)]
Phi_b <- bs(day, knots = kn, degree = 3, intercept = TRUE)
fit_b <- lm.fit(Phi_b, y)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
matplot(day, Phi_b, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, ylab = "", main = "Cubic B-spline basis"); abline(v = kn, lty = 3)
plot(day, y, pch = 20, col = "red", main = "Vancouver: B-spline fit"); lines(day, Phi_b %*% fit_b$coefficients, lwd = 3, col = "#003366")

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Smoothing Penalties: Roughness and \(\lambda\)
Use many basis functions, then penalize roughness. With a B-spline basis, Eilers and Marx’s P-splines replace \(\int[x'']^2\) by a difference penalty on the coefficients:
\[
\hat{\mathbf c}_\lambda = (\boldsymbol\Phi^\text{T}\boldsymbol\Phi + \lambda\mathbf{D}^\text{T}\mathbf{D})^{-1}\boldsymbol\Phi^\text{T}\mathbf{y},\qquad \mathbf{D}= \text{second-difference matrix}.
\]

yp <- precip[, "Vancouver"]
Phi <- bs(day, df = 40, degree = 3, intercept = TRUE); D <- diff(diag(ncol(Phi)), differences = 2)
psmooth <- function(lambda) { S <- Phi %*% solve(crossprod(Phi) + lambda * crossprod(D), t(Phi)); list(fit = S %*% yp, df = sum(diag(S))) }
plot(day, yp, col = "gray50", main = "Vancouver precipitation: P-spline smooths", xlab = "day", ylab = "mm")
cols <- c("#C0392B", "#003366", "#27AE60")
for (k in 1:3) lines(day, psmooth(c(0.1, 100, 1e5)[k])$fit, lwd = 3, col = cols[k])
legend("top", paste("lambda =", c(0.1, 100, 1e5)), col = cols, lwd = 3, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE)

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Choosing \(\lambda\): Generalized Cross-Validation
\[
\text{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{n\,\text{RSS}(\lambda)}{\big(n - \text{tr}\,\mathbf{S}_\lambda\big)^2}
\]

lams <- 10^seq(-2, 6, length = 40)
gcv <- sapply(lams, function(l) { s <- psmooth(l); 365 * sum((yp - s$fit)^2) / (365 - s$df)^2 })
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(lams, gcv, log = "x", type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "GCV"); abline(v = lams[which.min(gcv)], lty = 2)
best <- psmooth(lams[which.min(gcv)])
plot(day, yp, col = "gray50", main = sprintf("GCV choice: df = %.1f", best$df)); lines(day, best$fit, lwd = 3, col = "#003366")



The same idea as ridge regression (deck 04) with a structured penalty; LOOCV shortcut via the smoother matrix (deck 14).

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Bivariate Case: Tensor Product Bases
If \(\{\phi_i(x)\}_{i=1}^N\) and \(\{\psi_j(y)\}_{j=1}^M\) are bases in each dimension, the \(NM\) tensor product functions \(\phi_i(x)\psi_j(y)\) form a basis for surfaces: \(\bB = \bB_x\otimes\bB_y\).

zv <- volcano; xg <- seq(0, 1, length = nrow(zv)); yg <- seq(0, 1, length = ncol(zv))
Bx <- bs(xg, df = 10, intercept = TRUE); By <- bs(yg, df = 8, intercept = TRUE)
B <- kronecker(By, Bx)                                   # (87*61) x (10*8) tensor product design
cf <- qr.coef(qr(B), as.vector(zv)); zhat <- matrix(B %*% cf, nrow(zv))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
persp(xg, yg, zv, theta = 130, phi = 30, col = "#FFCC00", border = NA, shade = .5, main = "volcano (5307 values)")
persp(xg, yg, zhat, theta = 130, phi = 30, col = "#88A0C8", border = NA, shade = .5, main = "80 tensor B-spline coefficients")



Irregular domains: bivariate splines on triangulations (smoothness conditions across triangle edges).

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Singular Value Decomposition
\[
\mathbf{X}_{n\times m} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}^\text{T},\qquad \mathbf{U}^\text{T}\mathbf{U}= \mathbf{I},\ \mathbf{V}^\text{T}\mathbf{V}= \mathbf{I},\ \mathbf{S}= \text{diag}(s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots).
\]
Truncated SVD: \(\mathbf{X}_k = \mathbf{U}_k\mathbf{S}_k\mathbf{V}_k^\text{T}\) is the closest rank-\(k\) matrix to \(\mathbf{X}\) (Eckart-Young).

sv <- svd(volcano)
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
for (k in c(1, 2, 5, 20)) {
  Xk <- sv$u[, 1:k, drop = FALSE] %*% diag(sv$d[1:k], k) %*% t(sv$v[, 1:k, drop = FALSE])
  image(Xk, axes = FALSE, col = terrain.colors(60), main = sprintf("rank %d (%.1f%% energy)", k, 100 * sum(sv$d[1:k]^2) / sum(sv$d^2)))
}

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
section: PCA, Its Geometry, and the SVD Connection
text:
PCA, Its Geometry, and the SVD Connection

Find the direction \(\mathbf{v}\) with the greatest variation: \(\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1}\mathbf{v}^\text{T}\mathbf{X}^\text{T}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}\|^2\) (centered \(\mathbf{X}\)): the leading eigenvector of \(\mathbf{X}^\text{T}\mathbf{X}\).
From \(\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}^\text{T}\): \(\ \mathbf{X}^\text{T}\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}^2\mathbf{V}^\text{T}\), \(\ \mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\text{T}= \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}^2\mathbf{U}^\text{T}\), and \(\mathbf{U}= \mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}^{-1}\).


Xc <- scale(t(temp), scale = FALSE)                       # 35 stations x 365 days, centered
s <- svd(Xc); e <- eigen(crossprod(Xc), symmetric = TRUE)
c(max_eigenvalue_diff = max(abs(e$values[1:5] - s$d[1:5]^2)), PC_variance_share = round(s$d[1:3]^2 / sum(s$d^2), 3))

max_eigenvalue_diff  PC_variance_share1  PC_variance_share2  PC_variance_share3 
          2.328e-10           8.800e-01           8.500e-02           2.100e-02

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Functional PCA of Canadian Temperatures
Treat each station’s curve as one observation; the right singular vectors are the eigenfunctions \(\xi_k(t)\).

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
mu <- colMeans(t(temp))
matplot(day, s$v[, 1:3] * -1, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 3, col = c("#003366", "#C0392B", "#27AE60"),
        ylab = expression(xi[k](t)), main = "First three eigenfunctions")
legend("bottom", sprintf("PC%d (%.1f%%)", 1:3, 100 * s$d[1:3]^2 / sum(s$d^2)), col = c("#003366", "#C0392B", "#27AE60"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
plot(day, mu, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(-35, 25), ylab = "deg C", main = "Mean +/- 2 sd along PC1")
lines(day, mu + 2 * s$d[1] / sqrt(34) * s$v[, 1], lty = 2, lwd = 2); lines(day, mu - 2 * s$d[1] / sqrt(34) * s$v[, 1], lty = 3, lwd = 2)



PC1 is roughly “overall warmth” (more variation in winter); PC2 contrasts winter and summer (continental vs maritime climate).

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Station Scores

sc <- s$u[, 1:2] %*% diag(s$d[1:2])
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(-sc, type = "n", xlab = "PC1 score (warm ->)", ylab = "PC2 score")
text(-sc, labels = colnames(temp), cex = .8, col = ifelse(colnames(temp) %in% c("Vancouver", "Victoria", "Pr. Rupert"), "red", "#003366"))

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
section: FPCA with Smoothing and Missing Data
text:
FPCA with Smoothing and Missing Data

Raw SVD eigenfunctions are noisy when curves are noisy or sparsely observed.
Regularized FPCA (Huang, Shen and Buja, 2008): penalized rank-one approximation \[
\min_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\ \|\mathbf{X}- \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^\text{T}\|_F^2 + \lambda\,\mathbf{u}^\text{T}\mathbf{u}\ \mathbf{v}^\text{T}\boldsymbol\Omega\mathbf{v},
\] solved by alternating ridge-type updates; handles missing entries by fitting only observed cells.
Integrating data transformation, smoothing and missing data: https://fpca.shinyapps.io/fpca/ and the course code in FDAiR/shiny/.

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Independent Component Analysis (ICA) vs. PCA









PCA
ICA




Model
\(\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\), \(\mathbf{U}^\text{T}\mathbf{U}= \mathbf{I}\)
\(\mathbf{X}= \mathbf A\mathbf{S}\), \(\mathbf A\) invertible


Removes
correlations
correlations and higher-order dependence


Components
ordered by importance
equally important


Directions
orthogonal
not orthogonal




The cocktail party problem: unmix several microphone recordings into the original voices (course code: ICA/audio-demo.R, fastICA).


set.seed(4750); tt2 <- seq(0, 10, length = 1000)
S <- cbind(sin(2 * tt2), sign(sin(3 * tt2)))                 # two sources
X <- S %*% matrix(c(1, 1, -1, 2), 2)                         # two mixed "microphones"
ica <- fastICA::fastICA(X, n.comp = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
matplot(S, type = "l", lty = 1, main = "sources"); matplot(X, type = "l", lty = 1, main = "mixtures")
matplot(ica$S, type = "l", lty = 1, main = "ICA estimates")

title: A Journey Through Functional Data with R 〰️
text:
Summary


Functional data: smooth curves observed discretely with noise; think of each curve as one observation.
Represent with basis expansions (Fourier for periodic, B-splines in general); control roughness with a penalty and choose \(\lambda\) by GCV.
Surfaces: tensor-product bases; irregular domains: triangulations.
Variation: SVD/PCA \(\rightarrow\) functional PCA (eigenfunctions and scores); regularize for noisy or incomplete curves.

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
The Problem

Data \(\mathbf{X}\) is \(n\times p\); we see 2 (maybe 3) dimensions at a time.
Strategies:

Many low-dimensional views: scatterplot matrices, panels (conditioning)
Encode variables: color, shape, size, curves (Andrews), lines (parallel coordinates), glyphs (segments, stars)
Functions of two variables: surfaces and contours (densities!)
Projections: principal components

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
section: Example 5.3: Bivariate Normal Density with persp
text:
Example 5.3: Bivariate Normal Density with persp

f <- function(x, y, rho = 0.6) exp(-(x^2 - 2 * rho * x * y + y^2) / (2 * (1 - rho^2))) / (2 * pi * sqrt(1 - rho^2))
x <- y <- seq(-3, 3, length = 50)
z <- outer(x, y, f)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))
persp(x, y, z, theta = 45, phi = 30, expand = 0.6, ltheta = 120, shade = 0.75,
      ticktype = "detailed", col = "#FFCC00", border = NA, xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", zlab = "f(x, y)")
persp(x, y, z, theta = -30, phi = 15, expand = 0.6, col = "lightblue", border = "gray40")

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
section: Example 5.4: Adding Elements to a Perspective Plot
text:
Example 5.4: Adding Elements to a Perspective Plot
persp() returns the viewing transformation; trans3d() maps 3-d points to the plot.

par(mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))
M <- persp(x, y, z, theta = 45, phi = 30, expand = 0.5, col = "gray95", border = "gray80", box = FALSE)
# add a contour of f at its 50% level and the density along the line y = x
cl <- contourLines(x, y, z, levels = 0.08)[[1]]
lines(trans3d(cl$x, cl$y, rep(0.08, length(cl$x)), M), lwd = 3, col = "#C0392B")
s <- seq(-3, 3, length = 100)
lines(trans3d(s, s, f(s, s), M), lwd = 3, col = "#003366")
points(trans3d(0, 0, f(0, 0), M), pch = 19, cex = 2)

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Example 5.9: 2D Histogram

set.seed(4750)
Z <- MASS::mvrnorm(2000, c(0, 0), matrix(c(1, .7, .7, 1), 2))
bx <- cut(Z[, 1], breaks = seq(-4, 4, .5)); by <- cut(Z[, 2], breaks = seq(-4, 4, .5))
counts <- table(bx, by)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
image(seq(-3.75, 3.75, .5), seq(-3.75, 3.75, .5), unclass(counts), col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
      main = "2D histogram (bin counts)", xlab = "", ylab = "")
persp(seq(-3.75, 3.75, .5), seq(-3.75, 3.75, .5), unclass(counts) / (2000 * .25), theta = 40, phi = 30,
      col = "#FFCC00", shade = .4, main = "as a density", xlab = "x", ylab = "y", zlab = "")

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Example 5.10: Andrews Curves
Each observation \(\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip})\) becomes a curve on \([-\pi,\pi]\):
\[
f_i(t) = \frac{x_{i1}}{\sqrt2} + x_{i2}\sin t + x_{i3}\cos t + x_{i4}\sin 2t + x_{i5}\cos 2t + \cdots
\]

andrews <- function(v, t) {
  basis <- cbind(1 / sqrt(2), sapply(seq_len(length(v) - 1), function(j) {
    k <- ceiling(j / 2); if (j %% 2 == 1) sin(k * t) else cos(k * t) }))
  basis %*% v
}
Xs <- scale(iris[, 1:4]); tt <- seq(-pi, pi, length = 200)
curves <- apply(Xs, 1, andrews, t = tt)
matplot(tt, curves, type = "l", lty = 1, col = adjustcolor(c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60")[iris$Species], .35),
        xlab = "t", ylab = "f(t)", main = "Andrews curves: iris (scaled)")
legend("topright", levels(iris$Species), col = c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")




Andrews curves preserve Euclidean distances (up to a constant) because the basis is orthogonal on [-pi, pi]. Close points give close curves.

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Example 5.11: Parallel Coordinates

crabs <- MASS::crabs
x <- crabs[seq(5, 200, 5), ]                     # get every fifth obs.
x$group <- interaction(x$sp, x$sex)
MASS::parcoord(x[, 4:8] / x$CW, col = c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60", "orange")[x$group], lwd = 2,
               var.label = TRUE)
legend("topright", levels(x$group), col = c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60", "orange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")



Each variable is a vertical axis; each observation is a polyline. Measurements are divided by carapace width (CW) to remove the size effect.

text:
Example 5.12: Segment (Star) Plots

x <- crabs[seq(5, 200, 10), ]
stars(x[, 4:8] / x$CW, draw.segments = TRUE, labels = paste(x$sp, x$sex), nrow = 4,
      key.loc = c(14, 1.8), cex = .8, main = "Segment plots of crabs (scaled by CW)")

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
section: PCA: Projections That Keep the Most Variance
text:
PCA: Projections That Keep the Most Variance

Find orthogonal directions \(\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\dots\) maximizing \(\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v})\) subject to \(\|\mathbf{v}\| = 1\).
Solution: eigenvectors of the sample covariance (or correlation) matrix \(\mathbf{S}= \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol \Lambda\mathbf{V}^\text{T}\).
Equivalently, SVD of the centered data \(\tilde\mathbf{X}= \mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\text{T}\): scores \(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\), loadings \(\mathbf{V}\), variances \(d_j^2/(n-1)\).


Xc <- scale(USArrests)                         # use the correlation matrix
e <- eigen(cor(USArrests)); s <- svd(Xc)
rbind(eigen = e$values, svd = s$d^2 / (nrow(Xc) - 1))

      [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
eigen 2.48 0.9898 0.3566 0.1734
svd   2.48 0.9898 0.3566 0.1734

pc <- prcomp(USArrests, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pc)

Importance of components:
                        PC1   PC2    PC3    PC4
Standard deviation     1.57 0.995 0.5971 0.4164
Proportion of Variance 0.62 0.247 0.0891 0.0434
Cumulative Proportion  0.62 0.868 0.9566 1.0000

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Scree Plot and Loadings

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pc$sdev^2 / sum(pc$sdev^2), type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "component",
     ylab = "proportion of variance", main = "Scree plot")
lines(cumsum(pc$sdev^2) / sum(pc$sdev^2), type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2)
barplot(t(pc$rotation[, 1:2]), beside = TRUE, col = c("#003366", "#FFCC00"), legend.text = c("PC1", "PC2"),
        main = "Loadings")

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Example 5.14: The PC Biplot

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
biplot(pc, cex = c(0.7, 1), col = c("gray30", "#C0392B"), scale = 0)



States on the right have high crime; states on top are urban. Where is Wisconsin?

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
section: PCA as Dimension Reduction: Iris in 2 Dimensions
text:
PCA as Dimension Reduction: Iris in 2 Dimensions

pci <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)
p1 <- ggplot(data.frame(pci$x, Species = iris$Species), aes(PC1, PC2, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) + labs(title = sprintf("PC1-PC2 keep %.0f%% of the variance",
                                               100 * sum(pci$sdev[1:2]^2) / 4))

  geom_point(size = 2) + labs(title = "Two raw variables")

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Other Approaches (Rizzo 5.8)

Projection pursuit and grand tours (tourr): look for “interesting” (non-normal) projections
Multidimensional scaling (cmdscale): embed a distance matrix in 2-d
t-SNE / UMAP: nonlinear embeddings (great for exploration, careful with interpretation)
Interactive graphics: plotly, ggiraph, shiny (next week!)


mds <- cmdscale(dist(scale(USArrests)), k = 2)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)); plot(mds, type = "n", xlab = "MDS 1", ylab = "MDS 2")
text(mds, labels = state.abb[match(rownames(USArrests), state.name)], cex = .8)

title: Visualization of Multivariate Data 🎨
text:
Summary


Many small views: pairs, splom, conditioning panels.
Correlation structure: reordered correlation heatmaps.
Surfaces: persp, wireframe, contour, image, filled.contour, 2-d histograms.
Encodings: Andrews curves, parallel coordinates, segment/star glyphs.
PCA via eigen / SVD; scree plots and biplots; MDS as a cousin.

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Optimization Is Everywhere in Statistics

Maximum likelihood: \(\hat\theta = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_\theta\ell(\theta)\)
Least squares, ridge, lasso: \(\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\beta\ \text{RSS} + \lambda\,\text{penalty}\)
K-means: \(\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{C, c}\sum_k\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i - c_k\|^2\)
Neural networks: minimize a loss over millions of weights
Bandwidth selection: minimize UCV\((h)\)

R’s toolbox: optimize() (1-d), optim() (Nelder-Mead, BFGS, CG, L-BFGS-B, SANN, Brent), nlm(), nlminb(), constrOptim(), boot::simplex() (linear programming).

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Example 14.1: One-Dimensional Optimization
Maximize \(f(x) = \dfrac{\log(x + \log x)}{\log(1+x)}\).

f <- function(x) log(x + log(x)) / log(1 + x)
curve(f(x), from = 2, to = 15, ylab = "f(x)", lwd = 3, col = "#003366")
opt <- optimize(f, lower = 4, upper = 8, maximum = TRUE)
abline(v = opt$maximum, lty = 2, col = 2)

unlist(opt)

  maximum objective 
    5.792     1.055 



optimize uses golden-section search with parabolic interpolation; it finds a local optimum in the interval.

title: Optimization ⛰️
Optimization ⛰️
text:
Newton’s Method and Its Relatives
To maximize \(\ell(\theta)\), solve \(\nabla\ell(\theta) = \mathbf 0\) with Newton’s method:
\[
\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \big[\nabla^2\ell(\theta_k)\big]^{-1}\nabla\ell(\theta_k).
\]









Method
Uses
Convergence
Cost per step




Gradient ascent
\(\nabla\ell\)
linear
cheap


Newton-Raphson
\(\nabla\ell\), \(\nabla^2\ell\)
quadratic (near optimum)
Hessian + solve


Fisher scoring
\(\nabla\ell\), \(\mathcal I(\theta)\)
~quadratic
expected information


Quasi-Newton (BFGS)
\(\nabla\ell\), Hessian approximation
superlinear
cheap updates


Nelder-Mead
\(\ell\) only
slow, robust
function evaluations

title: Optimization ⛰️
section: Gradient Descent vs. Newton on a Quadratic
text:
Gradient Descent vs. Newton on a Quadratic

A <- matrix(c(3, 1.4, 1.4, 1), 2); b <- c(1, 1)
fq <- function(x) 0.5 * sum(x * (A %*% x)) - sum(b * x)        # minimum at solve(A, b)
gq <- function(x) as.vector(A %*% x - b)
gd <- function(x, step = 0.25, n = 40) { path <- x; for (k in 1:n) { x <- x - step * gq(x); path <- rbind(path, x) }; path }
nt <- function(x, n = 2) { path <- x; for (k in 1:n) { x <- x - solve(A, gq(x)); path <- rbind(path, x) }; path }
g1 <- seq(-3, 3, length = 100); z <- outer(g1, g1, Vectorize(function(u, v) fq(c(u, v))))
contour(g1, g1, z, nlevels = 25, col = "gray60", asp = 1, xlab = expression(theta[1]), ylab = expression(theta[2]))
lines(gd(c(-2.5, 2.5)), type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#C0392B", lwd = 2)
lines(nt(c(-2.5, 2.5)), type = "b", pch = 17, col = "#003366", lwd = 3, cex = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("gradient descent (40 steps)", "Newton (1 step!)"), col = c("#C0392B", "#003366"), lwd = 2, pch = c(19, 17), bty = "n")

title: Optimization ⛰️
section: Example 14.2: MLE for the Gamma Distribution
text:
Example 14.2: MLE for the Gamma Distribution
\[
\ell(r,\lambda) = nr\log\lambda + (r-1)\sum\log x_i - \lambda\sum x_i - n\log\Gamma(r).
\]
Setting \(\partial\ell/\partial\lambda = 0\) gives \(\lambda = r/\bar x\); substituting, \(r\) solves the one-dimensional equation
\[
\log r - \psi(r) = \log\bar x - \overline{\log x}\qquad(\psi = \text{digamma}).
\]

set.seed(4750); m <- 2000; est <- matrix(0, m, 2); n <- 200; r <- 5; lambda <- 2
obj <- function(r, x) log(r) - digamma(r) - (log(mean(x)) - mean(log(x)))
for (i in 1:m) {
  x <- rgamma(n, shape = r, rate = lambda)
  u <- uniroot(obj, lower = .001, upper = 10e5, x = x)
  est[i, ] <- c(u$root, u$root / mean(x))
}
colMeans(est)              # close to (5, 2)

[1] 5.064 2.028

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Example 14.3: Two-Dimensional Optimization with optim

LL <- function(theta, sx, slogx, n) {
  r <- theta[1]; lambda <- theta[2]
  loglik <- n * r * log(lambda) + (r - 1) * slogx - lambda * sx - n * log(gamma(r))
  -loglik
}
set.seed(4750); n <- 200; x <- rgamma(n, shape = 5, rate = 2)
optim(c(1, 1), LL, sx = sum(x), slogx = sum(log(x)), n = n)[c("par", "value", "counts", "convergence")]

$par
[1] 4.670 1.879

$value
[1] 296.6

$counts
function gradient 
      73       NA 

$convergence
[1] 0



Default method is Nelder-Mead (no derivatives). Try method = "BFGS" with an analytic gradient:


grLL <- function(theta, sx, slogx, n) {
  r <- theta[1]; lambda <- theta[2]
  -c(n * log(lambda) + slogx - n * digamma(r), n * r / lambda - sx)
}
fit <- optim(c(1, 1), LL, grLL, sx = sum(x), slogx = sum(log(x)), n = n, method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = c(1e-4, 1e-4), hessian = TRUE)
rbind(estimate = fit$par, se = sqrt(diag(solve(fit$hessian))))

           [,1]   [,2]
estimate 4.6701 1.8795
se       0.4513 0.1918

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Reparametrize Instead of Constraining
\(r, \lambda > 0\): optimize over \((\log r, \log\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^2\); use lgamma() not log(gamma()) (Ch 13!).

LL2 <- function(eta, x) -sum(dgamma(x, shape = exp(eta[1]), rate = exp(eta[2]), log = TRUE))
fit2 <- optim(c(0, 0), LL2, x = x, method = "BFGS")
exp(fit2$par)

[1] 4.670 1.879



Good practice for optim: sensible starting values (MOM!), unconstrained parametrization, analytic gradients when available, check convergence == 0, and try more than one start.

title: Optimization ⛰️
section: Example 14.4: MLE for a Quadratic Form (a Mixture)
text:
Example 14.4: MLE for a Quadratic Form (a Mixture)
\(Y = \lambda_1X_1^2 + \cdots + \lambda_kX_k^2\) in distribution is an equal mixture of Gamma\(\big(\tfrac12, \tfrac1{2\lambda_j}\big)\) (here \(k = 3\), \(\sum\lambda_j = 1\)).

LL <- function(lambda, y) {
  lambda3 <- 1 - sum(lambda)
  f1 <- dgamma(y, shape = 1/2, rate = 1 / (2 * lambda[1]))
  f2 <- dgamma(y, shape = 1/2, rate = 1 / (2 * lambda[2]))
  f3 <- dgamma(y, shape = 1/2, rate = 1 / (2 * lambda3))
  f <- f1 / 3 + f2 / 3 + f3 / 3        # density of mixture
  return(-sum(log(f)))                 # returning -loglikelihood
}
set.seed(9); m <- 2000
lambda <- c(.6, .25, .15)              # rate is 1/(2lambda)
lam <- sample(lambda, size = 2000, replace = TRUE)
y <- rgamma(m, shape = .5, rate = 1 / (2 * lam))
opt <- optim(c(.5, .3), LL, y = y)
c(opt$par, 1 - sum(opt$par))

[1] 0.5890 0.2505 0.1605



Next lecture: the EM algorithm solves the same problem (Example 14.5) without derivatives.

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Simulated Annealing (method = "SANN")
For rough or multimodal objectives, accept “uphill” moves with probability \(e^{-\Delta/T}\) and lower the temperature \(T\).

rough <- function(x) (x[1]^2 + x[2]^2) / 20 - cos(3 * x[1]) * cos(3 * x[2])   # many local minima
set.seed(4750)
starts <- matrix(runif(20, -4, 4), 10)
bfgs <- apply(starts, 1, function(s) optim(s, rough, method = "BFGS")$value)
sann <- apply(starts, 1, function(s) optim(s, rough, method = "SANN", control = list(maxit = 5000))$value)
boxplot(list(BFGS = bfgs, SANN = sann), horizontal = TRUE, col = c("#88A0C8", "#FFCC00"),
        main = "Final objective from 10 random starts (global min = -1)")

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Example 14.6: The Simplex Algorithm
Maximize \(2x + 2y + 3z\) subject to \(-2x + y + z\le 1\), \(\ 4x - y + 3z\le 3\), \(\ x, y, z\ge 0\).

If an optimum exists, it is attained at a vertex of the feasible polytope; the simplex method moves from vertex to vertex in the direction of greatest increase.


library(boot)
A1 <- rbind(c(-2, 1, 1), c(4, -1, 3)); b1 <- c(1, 3); a <- c(2, 2, 3)
s <- simplex(a = a, A1 = A1, b1 = b1, maxi = TRUE)
s$soln; s$value

x1 x2 x3 
 2  5  0 


 b 
14 



The solution is \((x, y, z) = (2, 5, 0)\) with value 14. Can you verify the two constraints are active?

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Example 14.7: Solving the Morra Game
3-finger Morra: each player shows 1-3 fingers and guesses the opponent’s number; a correct guess wins the total shown. 9 pure strategies; a zero-sum game solved by two linear programs (one per player).

solve.game <- function(A) {
  min.A <- min(A); A <- A - min.A; max.A <- max(A); A <- A / max(A)   # so that v >= 0
  m <- nrow(A); n <- ncol(A); it <- n^3
  a <- c(rep(0, m), 1)                          # maximize v for player 1
  A1 <- -cbind(t(A), rep(-1, n)); b1 <- rep(0, n)
  A3 <- t(as.matrix(c(rep(1, m), 0))); b3 <- 1
  sx <- simplex(a = a, A1 = A1, b1 = b1, A3 = A3, b3 = b3, maxi = TRUE, n.iter = it)
  a <- c(rep(0, n), 1)                          # minimize v for player 2
  A1 <- cbind(A, rep(-1, m)); b1 <- rep(0, m)
  A3 <- t(as.matrix(c(rep(1, n), 0))); b3 <- 1
  sy <- simplex(a = a, A1 = A1, b1 = b1, A3 = A3, b3 = b3, maxi = FALSE, n.iter = it)
  list("A" = A * max.A + min.A, "x" = sx$soln[1:m], "y" = sy$soln[1:n], "v" = sx$soln[m + 1] * max.A + min.A)
}
A <- matrix(c(0, -2, -2, 3, 0, 0, 4, 0, 0,  2, 0, 0, 0, -3, -3, 4, 0, 0,  2, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, -4, -4,
             -3, 0, -3, 0, 4, 0, 0, 5, 0,  0, 3, 0, -4, 0, -4, 0, 5, 0,  0, 3, 0, 0, 4, 0, -5, 0, -5,
             -4, -4, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0, 0, 6,  0, 0, 4, -5, -5, 0, 0, 0, 6,  0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 5, -6, -6, 0), 9, 9)
sol <- solve.game(A)
round(cbind(player1 = sol$x, player2 = sol$y), 7); sol$v

   player1 player2
x1  0.0000  0.0000
x2  0.0000  0.0000
x3  0.4098  0.4098
x4  0.0000  0.0000
x5  0.3279  0.3279
x6  0.0000  0.0000
x7  0.2623  0.2623
x8  0.0000  0.0000
x9  0.0000  0.0000


x10

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Python Supplement: scipy.optimize
import numpy as np
from scipy import optimize, special, stats
x = stats.gamma(a=5, scale=1/2).rvs(size=200, random_state=4750)
def nll(eta):
    r, lam = np.exp(eta)
    return -np.sum(stats.gamma.logpdf(x, a=r, scale=1/lam))
fit = optimize.minimize(nll, x0=[0, 0], method="BFGS")
print(np.exp(fit.x))
res = optimize.linprog(c=[-2, -2, -3], A_ub=[[-2, 1, 1], [4, -1, 3]], b_ub=[1, 3])   # Example 14.6
print(res.x, -res.fun)

title: Optimization ⛰️
text:
Summary


1-d: optimize() (golden section + parabolic interpolation); roots of the score: uniroot().
Multi-d: optim(); Nelder-Mead (default), BFGS/L-BFGS-B with gradients, SANN for rough surfaces.
Newton is fast near the optimum; gradient methods are cheap per step; quasi-Newton is the usual compromise.
Reparametrize to remove constraints, use log-scale functions, start from MOM.
Linear programs (boot::simplex): optima at vertices; zero-sum games.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Don’t Confuse Clustering and Classification!


Classification (supervised)

Data whose groups are known
Learn what differentiates the groups (a classification function) to classify future data
e.g. handwritten digits 0-9 with labels


Clustering (unsupervised)

Groups are unknown and undefined
Learn the groups themselves, as well as what differentiates them

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Dissimilarity and Within-Cluster Scatter

Observations \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) and dissimilarities \(d(X_i,X_j)\), e.g. \(X_i\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(d(X_i,X_j) = \|X_i - X_j\|_2^2\).
A clustering \(C\) assigns each \(X_i\) to a group \(C(i) = k\in\{1,\dots,K\}\); \(n_k\) points in group \(k\); \(d_{ij} = d(X_i,X_j)\).

The within-cluster scatter is
\[
W = \frac12\sum_{k=1}^K\frac1{n_k}\sum_{C(i)=k,\,C(j)=k} d_{ij}.
\]
Smaller \(W\) is better.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Simple Example: \(n = 5\), \(K = 2\)

P <- rbind(c(0.70, 0.02), c(0.95, 0.40), c(0.02, 0.70), c(0.38, 0.55), c(0.43, 0.97))
D <- as.matrix(dist(P))^2
round(D, 2)

     1    2    3    4    5
1 0.00 0.21 0.92 0.38 0.98
2 0.21 0.00 0.95 0.35 0.60
3 0.92 0.95 0.00 0.15 0.24
4 0.38 0.35 0.15 0.00 0.18
5 0.98 0.60 0.24 0.18 0.00

W <- function(cl, D) sum(sapply(unique(cl), function(k) sum(D[cl == k, cl == k]) / sum(cl == k))) / 2
c(red = W(c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2), D), blue = W(c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2), D))

   red   blue 
0.4330 0.2941 



The dist() function computes all pairwise distances (Euclidean by default; see method =).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Finding the Best Group Assignments
Why not search over all clusterings \(C\)? The number of possible assignments of \(n\) points into \(K\) nonempty groups is
\[
A(n,K) = \frac1{K!}\sum_{k=1}^K(-1)^{K-k}\binom Kk k^n .
\]

A <- function(n, K) sum((-1)^(K - (1:K)) * choose(K, 1:K) * (1:K)^n) / factorial(K)
c(A(10, 4), A(25, 4))

[1] 3.410e+04 4.677e+13



\(A(10,4) = 34{,}105\) and \(A(25,4)\approx 5\times10^{13}\): hopeless for realistic \(n\). We settle for an approximation.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Rewriting the Within-Cluster Scatter
For Euclidean data and \(d_{ij} = \|X_i - X_j\|_2^2\):
\[
\frac12\sum_{k=1}^K\frac1{n_k}\sum_{C(i)=k}\sum_{C(j)=k}\|X_i-X_j\|_2^2 = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i-\bar X_k\|_2^2,
\]
where \(\bar X_k = \frac1{n_k}\sum_{C(i)=k}X_i\). The right-hand side is the within-cluster variation.

cl <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2)
c(scatter = W(cl, D),
  wcv = sum(sapply(1:2, function(k) sum(sweep(P[cl == k, , drop = FALSE], 2, colMeans(P[cl == k, , drop = FALSE]))^2))))

scatter     wcv 
 0.2941  0.2941

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Rewriting the Minimization

For any \(Z_1,\dots,Z_m\), \(\sum_i\|Z_i - c\|_2^2\) is minimized by \(c = \bar Z\).
So minimizing the within-cluster variation is the same as minimizing the enlarged criterion

\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i - c_k\|_2^2 \quad\text{over both } C \text{ and } c_1,\dots,c_K\in\mathbb{R}^p.
\]

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
The K-Means Algorithm

Start with an initial guess for \(c_1,\dots,c_K\) (e.g. \(K\) random points). Repeat:

Minimize over \(C\): for each \(i\), find the closest center \(c_k\) to \(X_i\) and let \(C(i) = k\).
Minimize over \(c_1,\dots,c_K\): for each \(k\), let \(c_k = \bar X_k\), the average of points in group \(k\).

Stop when the within-cluster variation does not change.

In words: (1) label each point by its closest center; (2) replace each center by the average of its points.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
K-Means from Scratch

my_kmeans <- function(X, K, centers = X[sample(nrow(X), K), , drop = FALSE], maxit = 50) {
  history <- list(centers)
  for (it in 1:maxit) {
    d <- sapply(1:K, function(k) colSums((t(X) - centers[k, ])^2))   # n x K squared distances
    cl <- max.col(-d)                                                  # step 1: closest center
    new <- t(sapply(1:K, function(k) colMeans(X[cl == k, , drop = FALSE])))   # step 2: averages
    history[[it + 1]] <- new
    if (all(abs(new - centers) < 1e-10)) break
    centers <- new
  }
  wcv <- sum(sapply(1:K, function(k) sum(sweep(X[cl == k, , drop = FALSE], 2, centers[k, ])^2)))
  list(cluster = cl, centers = centers, wcv = wcv, iter = it, history = history)
}

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
K-Means Example: \(n = 300\), \(K = 3\)

set.seed(1)
X300 <- make_blobs(300, rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 1.4), c(1.2, 0.6)), sd = 0.22)
init <- rbind(c(1.2, 1.3), c(0.2, -0.3), c(0.3, 0.2))
fit <- my_kmeans(X300, 3, centers = init)
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
cols <- c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60")
for (it in c(1, 2, 3, length(fit$history))) {
  cen <- fit$history[[it]]
  cl <- max.col(-sapply(1:3, function(k) colSums((t(X300) - cen[k, ])^2)))
  plot(X300, col = if (it == 1) "gray60" else adjustcolor(cols[cl], .4), pch = 20,
       main = if (it == 1) "Initial centers" else paste("Iteration", it - 1))
  points(cen, pch = 19, cex = 2.5, col = cols)
}

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Properties of K-Means

Within-cluster variation decreases with each iteration: if \(W_t\) is the value at iteration \(t\), then \(W_{t+1}\le W_t\).
The algorithm always converges, no matter the initial centers. (In at most \(K^n\) iterations. Why?)
The final clustering depends on the initial centers. Run K-means multiple times (e.g. 10 random starts) and keep the solution with the smallest within-cluster variation.
K-means is not guaranteed to find the global minimizer (that would require all \(A(n,K)\) assignments!).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Multiple Runs: \(n = 250\), \(K = 4\)

set.seed(11)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))
cols4 <- c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60", "#C2185B")
for (r in 1:3) {
  f <- my_kmeans(X250, 4)
  plot(X250, col = adjustcolor(cols4[f$cluster], .5), pch = 20, main = sprintf("WCV = %.1f", f$wcv))
  points(f$centers, pch = 19, cex = 2.5, col = cols4)
}



In R, kmeans(X, centers = K, nstart = 20) does this automatically (Hartigan-Wong algorithm by default).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
kmeans() in R and Standardization

km <- kmeans(X250, centers = 4, nstart = 20)
km$tot.withinss; km$size

[1] 13.57


[1] 61 65 65 59



K-means uses Euclidean distance: variables on larger scales dominate. Usually scale() the variables first.


set.seed(4750)
table(kmeans(scale(iris[, 1:4]), 3, nstart = 20)$cluster, iris$Species)

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
K-Medoids (PAM)

K-means centers are averages (not data points) and are sensitive to outliers.
K-medoids restricts the centers to be data points (medoids) and works with any dissimilarity.


library(cluster)
pm <- pam(X250, k = 4)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1))
plot(X250, col = adjustcolor(cols4[pm$clustering], .5), pch = 20, main = "PAM (K-medoids)")
points(pm$medoids, pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 4)
plot(X250, col = adjustcolor(cols4[km$cluster], .5), pch = 20, main = "K-means")
points(km$centers, pch = 4, cex = 3, lwd = 4)

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
From K-Means to Hierarchical Clustering
Recall two properties of K-means (K-medoids):

It fits exactly \(K\) clusters (as specified).
The final assignment depends on the chosen initial centers.

Given pairwise dissimilarities \(d_{ij}\), hierarchical clustering produces a consistent result without choosing initial positions or the number of clusters.

The catch: we must choose a way to measure dissimilarity between groups, called the linkage.
The result is a sequence of clusterings: at one end all points are in their own cluster, at the other end all points are in one cluster.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Agglomerative vs. Divisive


Agglomerative (bottom-up)

Start with all points in their own group
Until there is only one cluster, repeatedly merge the two groups with the smallest dissimilarity


Divisive (top-down)

Start with all points in one cluster
Until all points are in their own cluster, repeatedly split the group into two, resulting in the biggest dissimilarity


Agglomerative strategies are simpler; we focus on them (hclust()). Divisive: cluster::diana().

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Simple Example and the Dendrogram

P7 <- rbind(c(.88, .92), c(.27, .66), c(.38, .63), c(.57, .1), c(.89, .3), c(.2, .2), c(.88, .7))
hc7 <- hclust(dist(P7), method = "complete")
hc7$merge                              # the merge sequence (negative = singletons)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]   -2   -3
[2,]   -1   -7
[3,]   -4   -5
[4,]   -6    1
[5,]    3    4
[6,]    2    5

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(P7, pch = 1, cex = 2, xlab = "Dimension 1", ylab = "Dimension 2", xlim = c(.1, 1)); text(P7, labels = 1:7, pos = 2)
plot(hc7, main = "Dendrogram", xlab = "", sub = "")

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
What’s a Dendrogram?
A tree that displays the hierarchical sequence of clusterings:

Each node represents a group; each leaf is a singleton; the root contains the whole data set.
Each internal node has two daughters: the groups that were merged to form it.
With leaves at height zero, each internal node is drawn at a height proportional to the dissimilarity between its two daughters.
Cutting the dendrogram horizontally partitions the data into clusters: cutree(hc, h = ) or cutree(hc, k = ).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Linkages

Points \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), dissimilarities \(d_{ij}\) (here \(d_{ij} = \|X_i - X_j\|_2\), distance not squared).
Groups \(G, H\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\). A linkage is a function \(d(G,H)\) returning a dissimilarity score between groups.


Agglomerative clustering: start with all points in their own group; until there is only one cluster, merge the two groups \(G, H\) with the smallest \(d(G,H)\).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Single Linkage
Nearest-neighbor linkage: the smallest dissimilarity between two points in opposite groups, \[
d_{\text{single}}(G,H) = \min_{i\in G,\,j\in H}d_{ij}.
\]

Cut interpretation: for each point \(X_i\), there is another point \(X_j\) in its cluster with \(d_{ij}\le 0.9\).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Complete Linkage
Furthest-neighbor linkage: the largest dissimilarity between two points in opposite groups, \[
d_{\text{complete}}(G,H) = \max_{i\in G,\,j\in H}d_{ij}.
\]

Cut interpretation: for each point \(X_i\), every other point \(X_j\) in its cluster satisfies \(d_{ij}\le 5\).

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Average Linkage
The average dissimilarity over all pairs in opposite groups, \[
d_{\text{average}}(G,H) = \frac1{n_G\cdot n_H}\sum_{i\in G,\,j\in H}d_{ij}.
\]

Cut interpretation: there really isn’t a good one!

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
section: Shortcomings of Single, Complete, and Average Linkage
text:
Shortcomings of Single, Complete, and Average Linkage

Single linkage suffers from chaining: to merge two groups, only one pair of points needs to be close. Clusters can be too spread out, not compact enough.
Complete linkage avoids chaining but suffers from crowding: a point can be closer to points in other clusters than to points in its own cluster.
Average linkage strikes a balance (relatively compact and relatively far apart), but

it is not clear what properties the clusters have when we cut the tree, and
results can change with a monotone increasing transformation of the \(d_{ij}\) (single and complete are unchanged).



par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
for (pw in 1:2) plot(X60, col = c("#C0392B", "#2E5BBA", "#27AE60")[cutree(hclust(d60^pw, "average"), k = 3)],
                     pch = 1, lwd = 2, main = c("Avg linkage: distance", "Avg linkage: distance^2")[pw])

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Centroid Linkage
Commonly used in biology (Eisen et al., 1998). With group averages \(\bar X_G\), \(\bar X_H\): \[
d_{\text{centroid}}(G,H) = \|\bar X_G - \bar X_H\|_2.
\]

hc_c <- hclust(d60^2, method = "centroid")      # R's centroid method expects squared distances
sum(diff(hc_c$height) < 0)                      # number of inversions in the merge heights

[1] 5

par(mar = c(1, 4, 1, 1)); plot(hc_c, labels = FALSE, main = "", xlab = "", sub = "")



Simple, but can produce dendrograms with inversions (a merge lower than the previous one), there is no cut interpretation, and answers change under monotone transformations.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Minimax Linkage
Define the radius of a group around \(X_i\) as \(r(X_i, G) = \max_{j\in G}d_{ij}\). Then \[
d_{\text{minimax}}(G,H) = \min_{i\in G\cup H}r(X_i, G\cup H),
\] the smallest radius encompassing all points in \(G\) and \(H\); the minimizer \(X_c\) is the prototype (Bien and Tibshirani, 2011).

Cut interpretation: each point is within \(h\) of the center (a data point!) of its cluster.
No inversions; unchanged by monotone transformations; the hierarchical analogue of K-medoids.


hc_mm <- protoclust::protoclust(d60)
plot(hc_mm, labels = FALSE, main = "Minimax linkage (protoclust)", xlab = "", sub = "")

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
This Is a Hard Problem

Sometimes \(K\) is known ahead of time (segment customers for \(K\) salespeople; vector quantization with \(K\) codewords).
Other times \(K\) is implicitly defined by cutting a tree at a given height.
In most exploratory applications \(K\) is unknown. What is the “right” value of \(K\)?

Why is it hard? It is hard for humans to perform (unless the data are low-dimensional) and just as hard to explain what we are looking for. Why is it important? E.g., \(K=2\) vs. \(K=3\) subtypes of breast cancer is a big scientific difference.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Within-Cluster Variation Just Keeps Decreasing
\[
W(K) = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{C(i)=k}\|X_i - \bar X_k\|_2^2
\]

set.seed(4750)
fits <- lapply(1:10, function(k) kmeans(X250, k, nstart = 20))
Wk <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "tot.withinss"); Bk <- sapply(fits, `[[`, "betweenss")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(X250, pch = 20, col = "gray50"); points(fits[[4]]$centers, pch = 19, cex = 2.5, col = cols4)
plot(1:10, Wk, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "Within-cluster variation")

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Between-Cluster Variation
\[
B(K) = \sum_{k=1}^K n_k\|\bar X_k - \bar X\|_2^2,\qquad \bar X = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i
\]

Bigger \(B\) is better, but \(B(K)\) just keeps increasing with \(K\).
Note \(W(K) + B(K) = \text{TSS}\), constant!


plot(1:10, Bk, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "Between-cluster variation")

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
The CH Index (Calinski and Harabasz, 1974)
We want simultaneously a small \(W\) and a large \(B\):
\[
\text{CH}(K) = \frac{B(K)/(K-1)}{W(K)/(n-K)},\qquad \hat K = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{K\in\{2,\dots,K_{\max}\}}\text{CH}(K).
\]

n <- nrow(X250); K <- 2:10
CH <- (Bk[K] / (K - 1)) / (Wk[K] / (n - K))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(X250, pch = 20, col = adjustcolor(cols4[fits[[4]]$cluster], .5))
plot(K, CH, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "CH index"); abline(v = K[which.max(CH)], lty = 2, col = 2)



We would choose \(K = 4\). Problem: CH is not defined for \(K = 1\), so it can never choose “no clusters”.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
section: Two More Criteria: Silhouette and Gap Statistic
text:
Two More Criteria: Silhouette and Gap Statistic

sil <- sapply(2:10, function(k) mean(silhouette(fits[[k]]$cluster, dist(X250))[, "sil_width"]))
set.seed(4750)
gap <- clusGap(X250, FUNcluster = kmeans, K.max = 10, B = 50, nstart = 10)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(2:10, sil, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "K", ylab = "average silhouette width")
plot(gap, main = "Gap statistic")

maxSE(gap$Tab[, "gap"], gap$Tab[, "SE.sim"], method = "firstSEmax")

[1] 4




The gap statistic (Tibshirani, Walther, Hastie 2001) compares log W(K) with its expectation under a reference (uniform) distribution, and can choose K = 1.

title: K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering 🧩
text:
Summary


K-means: minimize within-cluster variation by alternating assignments and averages; use many random starts and standardize variables.
K-medoids (PAM): centers are data points; any dissimilarity.
Hierarchical: one tree, many clusterings; the linkage matters (single, complete, average, centroid, minimax, Ward).
Choosing \(K\): elbow of \(W(K)\), CH index, silhouette, gap statistic. No universal answer.



Apply K-means and hierarchical clustering (complete and average linkage) to scale(USArrests). Do the methods agree for \(K = 4\)?

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Random Variables and Moments (Rizzo 2.1)

cdf \(F_X(x) = P(X\le x)\): non-decreasing, right-continuous, \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F = 0\), \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F=1\)
Discrete: pmf \(f_X(x) = P(X=x)\); continuous: pdf \(f_X(x) = F_X'(x)\)
\(\mathrm{E}[X] = \int x\, dF(x)\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \mathrm{E}[X^2] - \mu^2\)
\(\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathrm{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]\), \(\rho(X,Y) = \dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\)


Uncorrelated does not imply independent, except when \((X, Y)\) is jointly normal.


For iid \(X_1,\dots,X_n\): \(\mathrm{E}[\bar X] = \mu\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar X) = \sigma^2/n\).

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
section: Conditional Expectation Rule and Conditional Variance Formula
text:
Conditional Expectation Rule and Conditional Variance Formula
\[
\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}\big[\mathrm{E}[X\mid Y]\big] \qquad (2.1)
\] \[
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{E}\big[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)\big] + \mathrm{Var}\big(\mathrm{E}[X\mid Y]\big) \qquad (2.2)
\]
Example (Poisson-Gamma mixture). \(X\mid \Lambda \sim\text{Poisson}(\Lambda)\), \(\Lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(r, \beta)\).

(2.1): \(\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[\Lambda] = r/\beta\)
(2.2): \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathrm{E}[\Lambda] + \mathrm{Var}(\Lambda) = r/\beta + r/\beta^2\)



set.seed(4750)
r <- 4; beta <- 2; n <- 1e5
lambda <- rgamma(n, shape = r, rate = beta)
x <- rpois(n, lambda)
rbind(simulation = c(mean = mean(x), var = var(x)),
      formulas   = c(r / beta, r / beta + r / beta^2))

            mean   var
simulation 1.997 3.003
formulas   2.000 3.000




This mixture is the negative binomial distribution: X ~ NegBin(r, p = beta/(1+beta)). Check with dnbinom.
HW 1 asks you to do exactly this for two other hierarchical models.

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
The Mixture Is Negative Binomial

k <- 0:12
obs <- as.numeric(table(factor(x, levels = k))) / n
barplot(rbind(obs, dnbinom(k, size = r, prob = beta / (1 + beta))), beside = TRUE,
        names.arg = k, col = c("#FFCC00", "#003366"), legend.text = c("simulated", "NegBin(4, 2/3)"),
        main = "Poisson-Gamma mixture")

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Some Discrete Distributions (Rizzo 2.2)



Binomial \(X\sim\text{Bin}(n,p)\): number of successes in \(n\) Bernoulli trials; \(np\), \(np(1-p)\)
Multinomial: counts in \(k\) categories
Geometric: \(P(X = x) = p q^x\), \(x=0,1,\dots\) (failures before first success); cdf \(1-q^{x+1}\) (Example 2.1)
Negative binomial \((r,p)\): failures before \(r\)th success; \(\binom{x+r-1}{r-1}p^rq^x\) (2.6)
Poisson\((\lambda)\): \(e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!\); mean = variance = \(\lambda\) (Example 2.2)



par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
k <- 0:15
plot(k, dbinom(k, 15, .4), type = "h", lwd = 5, main = "Bin(15, .4)", ylab = "")
plot(k, dgeom(k, .25), type = "h", lwd = 5, main = "Geom(.25)", ylab = "")
plot(k, dnbinom(k, 3, .4), type = "h", lwd = 5, main = "NegBin(3, .4)", ylab = "")
plot(k, dpois(k, 4), type = "h", lwd = 5, main = "Poisson(4)", ylab = "")

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Some Continuous Distributions (Rizzo 2.3)

Normal \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\): \(Z = (X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)\)
Gamma\((r,\lambda)\): \(f(x) = \frac{\lambda^r}{\Gamma(r)} x^{r-1}e^{-\lambda x}\); Exponential = Gamma\((1,\lambda)\); \(\chi^2(\nu)\) = Gamma\((\nu/2, 1/2)\)
Beta\((\alpha,\beta)\) on \((0,1)\); Uniform(0,1) = Beta(1,1)
Lognormal: \(\log X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\)
Student \(t(\nu)\) \(= Z/\sqrt{V/\nu}\), \(F(\nu_1,\nu_2)\) \(= (U/\nu_1)/(V/\nu_2)\)


set.seed(4750); z <- rnorm(1e5); v <- rchisq(1e5, df = 5)
tt <- z / sqrt(v / 5)
rbind(quantile(tt, c(.9, .95, .99)), qt(c(.9, .95, .99), df = 5))

       90%   95%   99%
[1,] 1.493 2.037 3.383
[2,] 1.476 2.015 3.365

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Memoryless Exponential (Examples 2.3 - 2.4)
\[
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(X>t).
\]

set.seed(2027); x <- rexp(1e6, rate = 0.5); s <- 2; t <- 3
c(conditional = mean(x[x > s] > s + t), unconditional = mean(x > t), exact = exp(-0.5 * t))

  conditional unconditional         exact 
       0.2233        0.2236        0.2231 



Two-parameter exponential with location \(\eta\): \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda(x-\eta)}\), \(x\ge\eta\) (shift a standard exponential).

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Multivariate Normal (Rizzo 2.4)
\[
f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\boldsymbol \Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol \mu)^\text{T}\boldsymbol \Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol \mu)\right\}
\]

Marginals and conditionals of a MVN are normal; linear transformations \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{b}\sim N(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol \mu+\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol \Sigma\mathbf{A}^\text{T})\)
If \(\mathbf{Z}\sim N_d(\mathbf 0, \mathbf{I})\) and \(\boldsymbol \Sigma= \mathbf{C}\mathbf{C}^\text{T}\), then \(\mathbf{X}= \boldsymbol \mu+ \mathbf{C}\mathbf{Z}\sim N_d(\boldsymbol \mu,\boldsymbol \Sigma)\) (Ch 3!)


Sigma <- matrix(c(1, .8, .8, 1), 2); C <- t(chol(Sigma))
set.seed(4750); Z <- matrix(rnorm(2 * 2000), nrow = 2)
X <- t(c(1, 2) + C %*% Z)
round(cov(X), 2)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,] 0.97 0.74
[2,] 0.74 0.92

plot(X, pch = 20, col = adjustcolor("#003366", .4), asp = 1, xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2")

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Limit Theorems (Rizzo 2.5)

WLLN: \(\bar X_n \xrightarrow{P}\mu\); SLLN: \(\bar X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu\)
CLT: \(\dfrac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{D} N(0,1)\) when \(\sigma^2<\infty\)


set.seed(4750)
par(mfrow = c(1, 4))
for (n in c(1, 5, 30, 100)) {
  xbar <- colMeans(matrix(rexp(n * 5000), nrow = n))
  hist((xbar - 1) / (1 / sqrt(n)), prob = TRUE, breaks = 40, main = paste("n =", n),
       xlab = "", col = "#FFCC00", xlim = c(-4, 4))
  curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "#003366")
}



Repeat with Cauchy data. What breaks, and why?

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Statistics (Rizzo 2.6): ecdf and Quantiles

ecdf \(F_n(x) = \frac1n\#\{i: x_i\le x\}\)
\(q\)-quantile: \(X_q = \inf\{x: F(x)\ge q\}\); R’s default quantile(type = 7) assigns \((k-1)/(n-1)\) to \(x_{(k)}\)


set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(25)
plot(ecdf(x), main = "ecdf of 25 N(0,1) draws vs true cdf", col = "#003366", lwd = 2)
curve(pnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

quantile(x, c(.25, .5, .75)); quantile(x, .5, type = 1)

    25%     50%     75% 
-0.8428 -0.3289  0.4457 


    50% 
-0.3289

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Bias, Standard Error, and MSE

\(\mathrm{bias}(\hat\theta) = \mathrm{E}[\hat\theta] - \theta\); unbiased if bias \(=0\)
\(\mathrm{se}(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)}\)
\(\mathrm{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \mathrm{E}[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2] = \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \mathrm{bias}^2(\hat\theta)\)

Example. For \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), compare \(S^2\) (divisor \(n-1\)) with \(\hat\sigma^2\) (divisor \(n\)):

set.seed(4750); n <- 10; sigma2 <- 4
sims <- replicate(1e5, { x <- rnorm(n, sd = 2); c(S2 = var(x), mle = var(x) * (n - 1) / n) })
rbind(bias = rowMeans(sims) - sigma2, MSE = rowMeans((sims - sigma2)^2))

            S2     mle
bias -0.006832 -0.4061
MSE   3.547734  3.0386



The biased estimator has the smaller MSE: the bias-variance trade-off we will see again in ridge regression and Bayes estimators.

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Maximum Likelihood (Examples 2.5 - 2.6)

\(L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid\theta)\), \(\hat\theta = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_\theta \log L(\theta)\)
Example 2.5: for \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\hat\mu = \bar x\), \(\hat\sigma^2 = \frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\)
Invariance (Example 2.6): if \(\hat\theta\) is the MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat\theta)\) is the MLE of \(g(\theta)\) (e.g. \(\hat\sigma = \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}\))


set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(50, mean = 5, sd = 2)
negll <- function(par) -sum(dnorm(x, par[1], exp(par[2]), log = TRUE))
fit <- optim(c(0, 0), negll)
c(mu_hat = fit$par[1], sigma_hat = exp(fit$par[2]),
  closed_form_mu = mean(x), closed_form_sigma = sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))

           mu_hat         sigma_hat    closed_form_mu closed_form_sigma 
            5.224             2.153             5.224             2.154 




We parametrize log(sigma) so the optimizer is unconstrained. More on optim in Chapter 14, and on MOM/MLE/Bayes in deck 05.

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Bayes’ Theorem and Bayesian Statistics (Rizzo 2.7)
\[
\pi(\theta\mid x) = \frac{f(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)}{\int f(x\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta} \;\propto\; \text{likelihood}\times\text{prior}
\]
Beta-Binomial: \(X\mid p\sim\text{Bin}(n,p)\), \(p\sim\text{Beta}(a,b)\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(p\mid x\sim\text{Beta}(a+x,\, b+n-x)\).

a <- 2; b <- 2; n <- 20; xobs <- 14
curve(dbeta(x, a, b), 0, 1, lwd = 3, lty = 2, ylim = c(0, 4.5), ylab = "density", xlab = "p")
curve(dbeta(x, a + xobs, b + n - xobs), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#003366")
abline(v = xobs / n, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("prior Beta(2,2)", "posterior Beta(16,8)", "MLE 14/20"), lty = c(2, 1, 1),
       col = c(1, "#003366", "red"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Markov Chains (Rizzo 2.8)

\(\{X_t\}\) with \(P(X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t = i, X_{t-1},\dots) = p_{ij}\); transition matrix \(\mathbf P = (p_{ij})\), rows sum to 1
\(n\)-step transitions: \(\mathbf P^n\); stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol\pi^\text{T}= \boldsymbol\pi^\text{T}\mathbf P\)

Example 2.7 (DNA mutation). \(p_{ii} = 1-3\alpha\), \(p_{ij} = \alpha\), \(\alpha = 0.1\).

alpha <- 0.1
P <- matrix(alpha, 4, 4); diag(P) <- 1 - 3 * alpha
matpow <- function(M, k) Reduce(`%*%`, replicate(k, M, simplify = FALSE))
round(matpow(P, 2), 4); round(matpow(P, 16), 4)

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,] 0.52 0.16 0.16 0.16
[2,] 0.16 0.52 0.16 0.16
[3,] 0.16 0.16 0.52 0.16
[4,] 0.16 0.16 0.16 0.52


       [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
[1,] 0.2502 0.2499 0.2499 0.2499
[2,] 0.2499 0.2502 0.2499 0.2499
[3,] 0.2499 0.2499 0.2502 0.2499
[4,] 0.2499 0.2499 0.2499 0.2502

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Example 2.8: Random Walk
\(X_{t+1} = X_t + \epsilon_t\), \(\epsilon_t = \pm 1\) with probability \(1/2\) each.

set.seed(4750)
walks <- replicate(5, cumsum(sample(c(-1, 1), 1000, replace = TRUE)))
matplot(walks, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, xlab = "t", ylab = expression(X[t]),
        main = "Five symmetric random walks")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)




Markov chains return in MCMC. Random walks return in Chapter 4 (random processes, Brownian motion).

title: Probability and Statistics Review 📊
text:
Summary


Conditional expectation / variance formulas: verify hierarchical models by simulation.
The d/p/q/r functions and the relationships between families.
MVN via Cholesky: our first generator recipe (Ch 3).
LLN and CLT explain why Monte Carlo works (Ch 6-7).
Bias / SE / MSE are the yardsticks for every estimator this semester.



HW 1, Extra Question: For \(X\sim\chi^2(\nu = N+1)\) with \(N\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), find \(\mathrm{E}[X]\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\) using (2.1)-(2.2) and by simulation.

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Density Estimation: The Problem

Given \(X_1,\dots,X_n\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}f\) (unknown), estimate \(f\) nonparametrically, i.e., without assuming a family.
Uses: exploratory analysis (modes, skewness), simulation (smoothed bootstrap), classification, mixture assessment (EM, Ch 14).
Accuracy: \(\text{MSE}(\hat f(x)) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat f(x)) + \mathrm{bias}^2(\hat f(x))\), integrated: \(\text{MISE} = \mathrm{E}\int(\hat f - f)^2\).


par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (h in c(1, 4, 12)) {
  hist(faithful$waiting, breaks = seq(40, 100, by = h), prob = TRUE, col = "#FFCC00",
       main = paste("bin width h =", h), xlab = "waiting time (min)")
}

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
section: The Histogram as a Density Estimate
text:
The Histogram as a Density Estimate
With bins \([t_k, t_{k+1})\) of width \(h\) and counts \(\nu_k\):
\[
\hat f(x) = \frac{\nu_k}{nh},\qquad t_k\le x < t_{k+1}.
\]

\(\mathrm{bias}(\hat f(x)) = O(h)\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat f(x)) = O\big(1/(nh)\big)\) \(\Rightarrow\) optimal \(h\propto n^{-1/3}\), MISE \(= O(n^{-2/3})\).

Three bin-width rules:








Rule
Bin width / classes
Notes




Sturges
\(k = 1 + \log_2 n\) classes
R default; oversmooths for large \(n\)


Scott
\(\hat h = 3.49\,\hat\sigma\,n^{-1/3}\)
normal reference, MISE-optimal for normal


Freedman-Diaconis
\(\hat h = 2\,\text{IQR}\,n^{-1/3}\)
robust to outliers

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Examples 12.1 - 12.3: Rules in Action

set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(1000)
c(Sturges = nclass.Sturges(x), Scott = nclass.scott(x), FD = nclass.FD(x))

Sturges   Scott      FD 
     11      19      25 

waiting <- faithful$waiting; n <- length(waiting)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (rule in c("Sturges", "Scott", "FD")) {
  hist(waiting, breaks = rule, prob = TRUE, col = "#88A0C8", main = paste("Old Faithful:", rule), xlab = "")
}

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Estimating \(f(x_0)\) from a Histogram (Example 12.2)

x0 <- 0.1; set.seed(4750); x <- rnorm(1000)
br <- pretty(x, n = nclass.scott(x)); h <- diff(br)[1]
k <- findInterval(x0, br)
c(fhat = sum(x >= br[k] & x < br[k + 1]) / (length(x) * h), true = dnorm(x0), h = h)

 fhat  true     h 
0.372 0.397 0.500

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Frequency Polygon (Example 12.4)
Linear interpolation of the histogram at the bin midpoints. Bias is \(O(h^2)\), optimal \(h = 2.15\,\sigma n^{-1/5}\) (normal reference).

h <- 2.15 * sd(waiting) * n^(-1/5)
br <- seq(min(waiting) - h, max(waiting) + h, by = h)
H <- hist(waiting, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
mids <- H$mids; dens <- H$density
plot(H, freq = FALSE, col = "gray90", main = "Frequency polygon: Old Faithful waiting times", xlab = "")
lines(c(mids[1] - h, mids, mids[length(mids)] + h), c(0, dens, 0), lwd = 3, col = "#003366")

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Averaged Shifted Histogram (ASH, Example 12.6)
Average \(m\) histograms with the same width \(h\) whose origins are shifted by \(h/m\): equivalent to a finer histogram with triangular weights.

ash1 <- function(x, h, m = 20, grid = seq(min(x) - h, max(x) + h, length = 400)) {
  delta <- h / m
  rowMeans(sapply(0:(m - 1), function(j) {
    br <- seq(min(x) - h - j * delta, max(x) + 2 * h, by = h)
    H <- hist(x, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
    H$density[findInterval(grid, br, all.inside = TRUE)]
  }))
}
grid <- seq(35, 105, length = 400)
plot(grid, ash1(waiting, h = 6, grid = grid), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#C0392B",
     xlab = "waiting", ylab = "density", main = "ASH: h = 6, m = 1 vs m = 20")
lines(grid, ash1(waiting, h = 6, m = 1, grid = grid), type = "s", col = "gray50")

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
From Histograms to Kernels
The kernel density estimator places a smooth bump at each observation:
\[
\hat f_h(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^nK\!\left(\frac{x - X_i}{h}\right),\qquad K\ge 0,\ \int K = 1.
\]

set.seed(4750); xs <- c(-1.5, -1, .2, .4, 1.8); h <- 0.4
gg <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length = 400)
bumps <- sapply(xs, function(xi) dnorm((gg - xi) / h) / (length(xs) * h))
matplot(gg, bumps, type = "l", lty = 2, col = "gray40", xlab = "x", ylab = "", main = "KDE = sum of bumps")
lines(gg, rowSums(bumps), lwd = 3, col = "#003366"); rug(xs, lwd = 3)

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Kernels


The choice of kernel matters little; the bandwidth \(h\) matters a lot.

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
section: Bias, Variance, and the Optimal Bandwidth
text:
Bias, Variance, and the Optimal Bandwidth
For a second-order kernel with \(\sigma_K^2 = \int t^2K(t)\,dt\) and \(R(g) = \int g^2\):
\[
\mathrm{bias}(\hat f_h(x))\approx\frac{h^2}{2}\sigma_K^2f''(x),\qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat f_h(x))\approx\frac{f(x)R(K)}{nh}
\]
\[
\text{AMISE}(h) = \frac{R(K)}{nh} + \frac{h^4}{4}\sigma_K^4R(f'')\quad\Rightarrow\quad h^* = \left(\frac{R(K)}{\sigma_K^4R(f'')n}\right)^{1/5}\propto n^{-1/5}.
\]

MISE rate \(O(n^{-4/5})\): better than the histogram’s \(O(n^{-2/3})\).
Normal reference (Gaussian \(K\), normal \(f\)): \(h = 1.06\,\hat\sigma\,n^{-1/5}\); Silverman’s rule bw.nrd0: \(h = 0.9\min(\hat\sigma, \text{IQR}/1.34)\,n^{-1/5}\).

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️

Example 12.7: KDE of Old Faithful Waiting Time

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (adj in c(.5, 1, 2)) {
  d <- density(waiting, adjust = adj)
  plot(d, main = sprintf("bw = %.2f (adjust = %.1f)", d$bw, adj), lwd = 2, col = "#003366")
  rug(waiting)

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Data-Driven Bandwidths: Cross-Validation
Least-squares (unbiased) cross-validation minimizes an unbiased estimate of \(\text{ISE} - \int f^2\):
\[
\text{UCV}(h) = \int\hat f_h^2 - \frac2n\sum_{i=1}^n\hat f_{h,(-i)}(X_i).
\]

ucv <- function(h, x) {
  n <- length(x); d <- outer(x, x, "-")
  int_f2 <- sum(dnorm(d, sd = sqrt(2) * h)) / n^2          # closed form for the Gaussian kernel
  loo <- (rowSums(dnorm(d / h)) - dnorm(0)) / ((n - 1) * h)
  int_f2 - 2 * mean(loo)
}
hs <- seq(1, 8, length = 60); u <- sapply(hs, ucv, x = waiting)
plot(hs, u, type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = "h", ylab = "UCV(h)"); abline(v = hs[which.min(u)], lty = 2, col = 2)

c(our_ucv = hs[which.min(u)], bw.ucv = bw.ucv(waiting))

our_ucv  bw.ucv 
  2.661   2.658 




bw.ucv uses a slightly different (binned) approximation, so values differ a little. bw.SJ (Sheather-Jones plug-in) is generally the recommended choice.

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
section: Examples 12.10 - 12.11: Boundaries and the Reflection Technique
text:
Examples 12.10 - 12.11: Boundaries and the Reflection Technique
For \(f\) supported on \([0,\infty)\), the KDE puts mass below 0 and underestimates \(f\) near the boundary.
Reflection: augment the sample with \(-X_i\), estimate, then fold: \(\hat f_R(x) = 2\hat f_{\{X,-X\}}(x)\) for \(x\ge0\).

set.seed(4750); x <- rexp(1000, 1)
d <- density(x, bw = 0.1, n = 1024)
xx <- c(x, -x)
g <- density(xx, bw = 0.1, n = 1024)
a <- seq(0, 6, .01); ux <- a[a < 3.5]
plot(d, xlim = c(-0.5, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 1.1), lwd = 2, main = "Exp(1): ordinary vs reflected KDE")
lines(g$x[g$x >= 0], 2 * g$y[g$x >= 0], lwd = 2, col = "#C0392B")
lines(ux, dexp(ux), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("ordinary KDE", "reflection", "true"), col = c(1, "#C0392B", 1), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
section: Example 12.12 - 12.13: Bivariate Frequency Table and Density Polygon
text:
Example 12.12 - 12.13: Bivariate Frequency Table and Density Polygon

bin2d <- function(x, breaks1 = "Sturges", breaks2 = "Sturges") {
  histg1 <- hist(x[, 1], breaks = breaks1, plot = FALSE)
  histg2 <- hist(x[, 2], breaks = breaks2, plot = FALSE)
  freq <- table(cut(x[, 1], histg1$breaks), cut(x[, 2], histg2$breaks))
  list(call = match.call(), freq = freq, breaks1 = histg1$breaks, breaks2 = histg2$breaks,
       mids1 = histg1$mids, mids2 = histg2$mids)
}
b <- bin2d(as.matrix(faithful))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
image(b$mids1, b$mids2, unclass(b$freq), col = hcl.colors(20, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE), xlab = "eruptions",
      ylab = "waiting", main = "2-d frequency table")
persp(b$mids1, b$mids2, unclass(b$freq), theta = 30, phi = 30, col = "#FFCC00", shade = .4,
      xlab = "eruptions", ylab = "waiting", zlab = "count", main = "density polygon")

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Example 12.15: Product Kernel Estimate
\[
\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{nh_1\cdots h_d}\sum_{i=1}^n\prod_{j=1}^dK\!\left(\frac{x_j - X_{ij}}{h_j}\right),\qquad h_j\propto\hat\sigma_jn^{-1/(d+4)}.
\]

set.seed(4750)
n <- 2000; p <- c(.2, .3, .5)
mu <- matrix(c(0, 1, 4, 0, 3, -1), 3, 2); Sigma <- diag(2)
i <- sample(1:3, replace = TRUE, prob = p, size = n)
xbvn <- t(sapply(i, function(k) MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu[k, ], Sigma)))
fhat <- MASS::kde2d(xbvn[, 1], xbvn[, 2], n = 60)        # Gaussian product kernel, normal-reference bandwidths
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
contour(fhat, main = "kde2d: contours"); points(mu, pch = 19, col = 2)
persp(fhat, phi = 30, theta = 20, d = 5, xlab = "x", ylab = "y", col = "#88A0C8", border = NA, shade = .5)




MASS::kde2d uses a Gaussian product kernel with bandwidth.nrd() in each coordinate (it divides h by 4 internally). ks::kde provides full bandwidth matrices and plug-in selectors.

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
section: The Curse of Dimensionality in Density Estimation
text:
The Curse of Dimensionality in Density Estimation

Optimal MISE rate for a KDE in \(d\) dimensions: \(O\big(n^{-4/(4+d)}\big)\).


d <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10)
data.frame(d = d, rate = paste0("n^(-", round(4 / (4 + d), 2), ")"),
           n_needed_for_1d_accuracy_of_n100 = round(100^((4 + d) / 5)))

   d      rate n_needed_for_1d_accuracy_of_n100
1  1  n^(-0.8)                              100
2  2 n^(-0.67)                              251
3  3 n^(-0.57)                              631
4  5 n^(-0.44)                             3981
5 10 n^(-0.29)                           398107



To match the accuracy of \(n = 100\) in 1-d, we need enormous samples in 10-d. This is why PCA/dimension reduction (Ch 5) is used before density estimation.

title: Probability Density Estimation 🏔️
text:
Summary


Histogram: \(h\propto n^{-1/3}\) (Scott, FD); Sturges oversmooths for large \(n\).
Frequency polygon and ASH: cheap, bias \(O(h^2)\).
KDE: \(\hat f = \frac1{nh}\sum K((x - X_i)/h)\); bandwidth is what matters: bw.nrd0, bw.SJ, cross-validation.
Boundaries need care (reflection); higher dimensions need much more data.

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Two Branches of Statistics

Descriptive statistics: collection, presentation, and description of sample data (tables, graphs, summaries).
Inferential statistics: interpreting descriptive results to make decisions and draw conclusions about the population.




Population: the entire group of interest
Sample: a part of the population selected to draw conclusions about the entire population

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Parameters vs. Statistics


Describing a population

Use Greek letters
Mean \(\mu\), standard deviation \(\sigma\), variance \(\sigma^2\), proportion \(p\)
For a given population there is only one true value of each
These fixed (unknown) values are parameters


Describing a sample

Sample mean \(\bar{x}\), standard deviation \(s\), variance \(s^2\), proportion \(\hat p\)
Different samples give different values
These random quantities are statistics



set.seed(4750)
population <- rgamma(1e5, shape = 2, rate = 0.5)       # a "population"
c(mu = mean(population), sigma = sd(population))

   mu sigma 
4.005 2.822 

replicate(5, mean(sample(population, 30)))           # five different sample means

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Combinatorial Methods

Multiplication rule. If an operation consists of \(k\) steps that can be done in \(n_1, n_2, \dots, n_k\) ways, the whole operation can be done in \(n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdots n_k\) ways.


Permutations of \(n\) distinct objects: \(n!\)
Permutations of \(n\) objects taken \(r\) at a time: \({}_nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}\)
Permutations with \(n_1, \dots, n_k\) objects of \(k\) kinds: \(\dfrac{n!}{n_1!\, n_2! \cdots n_k!}\)
Combinations: \(\dbinom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\), and the binomial theorem \((x+y)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} x^{n-r} y^r\)


factorial(5); factorial(10) / factorial(7); choose(10, 3)

[1] 120


[1] 720


[1] 120

factorial(11) / (factorial(4) * factorial(4) * factorial(2))   # MISSISSIPPI

[1] 34650

nrow(expand.grid(1:6, 1:6))    # two dice: 6 * 6 outcomes

[1] 36

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Sample Spaces and Events

Sample space \(S\): set of all possible outcomes; each outcome is a sample point.
Events are subsets of \(S\); use union \(A\cup B\), intersection \(A\cap B\), complement \(A'\).


S <- expand.grid(red = 1:6, green = 1:6)
A <- with(S, red + green == 7)          # event: the sum is 7
plot(S, pch = 19, col = ifelse(A, "red", "gray60"), cex = 2, asp = 1,
     main = "Two dice: the event {sum = 7}")

mean(A)                                 # P(A) = 6/36

[1] 0.1667

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Axioms and Basic Rules

Postulates. \(P(A) \ge 0\); \(P(S)=1\); for mutually exclusive \(A_1, A_2,\dots\), \(P(A_1\cup A_2\cup\cdots) = \sum_i P(A_i)\).


\(P(A') = 1 - P(A)\), \(\quad P(\varnothing) = 0\)
\(P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B)\)
\(P(A\cup B\cup C) = P(A)+P(B)+P(C) - P(A\cap B) - P(A\cap C) - P(B\cap C) + P(A\cap B\cap C)\)


B <- with(S, red == 6)
c(lhs = mean(A | B), rhs = mean(A) + mean(B) - mean(A & B))

   lhs    rhs 
0.3056 0.3056

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Conditional Probability, Independence, Bayes’ Rule

\(P(B\mid A) = \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}\), \(\quad\) \(A\) and \(B\) independent iff \(P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)\).
Total probability: if \(B_1,\dots,B_k\) partition \(S\), \(P(A) = \sum_i P(B_i)P(A\mid B_i)\).
Bayes’ rule: \(P(B_r\mid A) = \dfrac{P(B_r)P(A\mid B_r)}{\sum_i P(B_i)P(A\mid B_i)}\).


A test is 95% sensitive and 90% specific; prevalence is 2%. What is \(P(\text{disease}\mid +)\)?



prior <- 0.02; sens <- 0.95; spec <- 0.90
(prior * sens) / (prior * sens + (1 - prior) * (1 - spec))

[1] 0.1624

set.seed(1); n <- 1e6
D <- runif(n) < prior; pos <- ifelse(D, runif(n) < sens, runif(n) > spec)
mean(D[pos])          # simulation agrees

[1] 0.1618

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Discrete Random Variables

A random variable \(X\) is a real-valued function on \(S\).
pmf \(f(x) = P(X=x)\) with \(f(x)\ge 0\) and \(\sum_x f(x) = 1\).
cdf \(F(x) = P(X\le x) = \sum_{t\le x} f(t)\), a non-decreasing step function.


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
x <- 0:10
plot(x, dbinom(x, 10, 0.3), type = "h", lwd = 4, col = "#003366", ylab = "f(x)", main = "pmf: Bin(10, 0.3)")
plot(stepfun(x, c(0, pbinom(x, 10, 0.3))), verticals = FALSE, pch = 19, main = "cdf", ylab = "F(x)")

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Continuous Random Variables

pdf \(f(x)\ge 0\) with \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\) and \(P(a\le X\le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
For continuous \(X\): \(P(a\le X\le b) = P(a< X< b)\) since \(P(X=a)=0\).
cdf \(F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt\) and \(f(x) = F'(x)\).

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Distributions

Joint pmf/pdf \(f(x,y)\): \(P\big((X,Y)\in A\big) = \iint_A f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\)
Marginal: \(g(x) = \sum_y f(x,y)\) or \(\int f(x,y)\,dy\)
Conditional: \(f(x\mid y) = f(x,y)/h(y)\), \(h(y) \neq 0\)
\(X_1, \dots, X_n\) independent iff \(f(x_1,\dots,x_n) = f_1(x_1)\cdots f_n(x_n)\)


# joint pmf of (X, Y) = (first die, max of two dice)

title: Probability Review 🎲
text:
Expected Value and Moments

\(\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x x f(x)\) or \(\int x f(x)\,dx\); \(\quad\mathrm{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x)f(x)\) or \(\int g(x) f(x)\,dx\)
\(\mathrm{E}[aX+b] = a\mathrm{E}[X]+b\)
\(r\)th moment about the origin \(\mu_r' = \mathrm{E}[X^r]\); about the mean \(\mu_r = \mathrm{E}[(X-\mu)^r]\)
\(\sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}(X) = \mu_2 = \mu_2' - \mu^2\), \(\quad \mathrm{Var}(aX+b) = a^2\sigma^2\)


x <- 0:10; f <- dbinom(x, 10, 0.3)
EX <- sum(x * f); EX2 <- sum(x^2 * f)
c(EX = EX, VarX = EX2 - EX^2, theory = 10 * 0.3 * 0.7)

    EX   VarX theory 
   3.0    2.1    2.1
